📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing are on regular rotation in my home on my family’s screens, but not my own.
  • Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI is not a cozy game, but it has a substantial amount of cozy elements and mechanics.
  • And for some reason, I couldn’t start that process fast enough.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I admire the cozy sim genre. Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing are on regular rotation in my home on my family’s screens, but not my own. In an odd way, I find the genre stressful, arguably the opposite of its intended purpose. I will happily and cathartically guide Grace Ashcroft through the tense hallways of Rhodes Hill in Resident Evil Requiem, but Pokémon Pokopia’s seemingly endless list of to-dos makes me sweat. It’s just not my genre, and I have come to terms with that.

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI is not a cozy game, but it has a substantial amount of cozy elements and mechanics. Bird (and animal) watching, for example, is apparent and encouraged early in the experience. You can also fix up your somewhat dilapidated home from almost the moment you are let loose outside of the opening tutorial missions.

And for some reason, I couldn’t start that process fast enough.

I climbed to the roof to fix the leak and replaced all the stairs leading up to the home before I ever participated in the game’s namesake and stole a car. Normally, it’s the kind of interaction I skip or choose not to engage with, given the option. Or, I do the bare minimum to progress. Sure, I have all the options in the world to build and decorate a house and make it my own, but… that feels like a lot of work. And I am not an artist.

The “cozy” elements of Grand Theft Auto VI are admittedly different from those in a game like Pokopia or Animal Crossing. You’re not designing your home (though you can pick a paint color), but it feels similar, and I am trying to figure out why I enjoy it here as opposed to other games. Is it because Jason and Lucia are so instantly believable as human beings that I want their home to be nicer?

In a recent development, after some thought, I think it might just come down to Grand Theft Auto VI’s consistently impressive visual fidelity. Replacing the shingles on the roof, for example, offers a close-up look at Jason’s character model, and you can practically feel the texture of the asphalt while the heat of the sun beats down.

I don’t have confirmation, but it also just feels like someone at Rockstar did exhaustive research on what the process of replacing a roof shingle should look like, even if, I’m sure, it probably doesn’t quite work that way in the real world. Jason makes it look incredibly easy, to the point that it had me questioning if I should be climbing up to my own roof and taking care of some loose shingles myself. And you know what is a lot of fun? Watching someone who is good at something do the thing they’re good at.

I’m now into the driving and shooting part of the game (and enjoying that, too!), but I am shocked at how grateful I was to have the option to stay home and put up drywall.

Sources indicate that but what about everyone else? GTA 6 is nominated for Game of the Year at The Game Awards, so does it live up to that recommendation? Are the critics overwhelmingly enamoured with it? That's what we've been intrigued to find out.

So, here's what the critics are saying about GTA 6 so far:.

Industry observers note that "Somehow, GTA 6 lives up to the hype. Rockstar Games has crafted the most incredible open world I've ever experienced in a video game, packed with so much detail that I'll want to continue exploring it for months and likely years to come.".

Industry observers note that "GTA 6 is the deepest, densest, most accomplished open world since Red Dead Redemption 2. Rockstar has set a fresh sandbox standard here, with a world that feels alive and populated with real people; Leonida is a place where it appears almost anything can happen at any time.".

In a recent development, "A game so good I asked our tech team if I could somehow give it 11/10. GTA 6 is an absolute masterclass in genre-mashing. With meticulous detailing and levels of immersion that almost feel dangerous, it's steeped in steamy satire — with story beats that often cut close to home as they relish in laugh-out-loud absurdity. Given the state of the industry, it's sobering that we might never see another game like this again. Grand Theft Auto 6 is a cover-to-cover masterpiece without equal.".

"Grand Theft Auto VI is a generational game that stands toe-to-toe with many of the great crime stories and satires across other media. It showcases both the entertainment value of interactive play and the current high-water mark for technical and artistic detail in games. Hunt for and count up all the minor faults or foibles you like, but then note how you just spent another hour lost in this remarkable escape into criminality, wanton violence, egregious sex, and the elusive potential of true love.".

Sources indicate that "This game is the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach. GTA 6 is an astonishing open-world action game that I’d wager won’t be outdone until Grand Theft Auto 7.".

"GTA 6 is the highest-fidelity sandbox of its generation. Rockstar has built an open world of truly astonishing scale, scope, and quality. There's a degree of sophistication to everything GTA 6 does, and there's no aspect of the series' gameplay that hasn't been improved over past instalments.".

In a recent development, "I regularly find myself in love with video games, but it’s extraordinarily rare that I find myself in complete awe of them. Put simply, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played.".

"A game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale, Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action - and a load more after that.".

"Grand Theft Auto VI delivers a remarkably immersive and ambitious open-world experience, blending thrilling gameplay, diverse activities, and a compelling relationship between Jason and Lucia. While uneven storytelling, pacing issues, and occasional performance drops prevent it from reaching perfection, the richly realized world of Leonida and its extraordinary attention to detail make this an unforgettable crime adventure that largely lives up to its monumental expectations.".

"Grand Theft Auto VI is a great game that lives up to so much of the hype and expectations. Lucia and Jason are a well-written and compelling pair of protagonists, and the side characters you meet on their journey are great, even if the need to constantly raise the stakes across such a long story lessens its impact. You do have so much more freedom with how to tackle missions, though, and Leonida is a world filled with things to do and discover that will keep you coming back for a long time.".

As you can see, GTA 6 is a darling of the critics right now, and its initial rating on Metacritic sits at a whopping 99, which makes it the highest-rated game of 2026 (and literally the joint best game of all time if it keeps up this pace).

Industry observers note that it should be noted that the vast majority of reviews are for the PS5 version, but both the PlayStation and Xbox versions are both sitting at 99 as things stand. That figure will probably change, but not to any significant degree.

It has been revealed that history tells us that we should have always expected a mainline Grand Theft Auto game to get incredible review scores, but it was really hard to see how they'd live up to expectations with this one. Nevertheless, they've somehow done it!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Sims 4 players on PlayStation and Xbox have now caught up to their friends on PC, at least when it comes to the game’s Marketplace.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Sims 4 players on PlayStation and Xbox have now caught up to their friends on PC, at least when it comes to the game’s Marketplace. This new feature is essentially a hub for paid mods and other user-created content.

As often happens when long-established games introduce paid mods, The Sims 4’s wasn’t especially well-received, in part because of the introduction of a new premium currency - Moola - that is the only way to purchase any of that content.

The Moola denominations and prices are similar to many other in-game currencies, and the criticism around them is the same: they obfuscate the true value of items, and because of the way those denominations are structured, you’ll never be able to buy exactly what you need.

For most games, the subject of paid mods has always been fraught, and that's certainly true for The Sims 4. In the announcement blog post, Maxis said that the launch on consoles will work similarly to what PC players have seen, in that Kits will no longer be available to buy directly with real money on the PlayStation and Microsoft Stores. While Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs will remain, you’ll need to buy Moola if you want to acquire Kits going forward.

Industry observers note that interestingly, however, EA seems to have changed its mind somewhat on the Kits situation. A recently leaked memo (via SimsCommunity), appears to show that the publisher intends on making Kits available for purchase directly again, without the need for Moola.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, this only appears to affect the PC version, with the reversion reportedly forthcoming on both the EA App as well as Steam. Indeed, according to the same report, the change has already taken place on the former, with the latter following on April 20.

Considering the Marketplace only just released on consoles, the company may wait to see if the decision to remove Kits from console platform marketplaces will be as poorly received as it has been on PC.

If you’re looking to jump back into The Sims 4 to check out all the latest paid content, make sure you’re well-equipped with our list of Sims 4 cheats and debug options, or this one specifically for the Royalty & Legacy expansion cheats.

  • "A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations," isn't part of the marketing spiel for either of those games.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xbox have confirmed that Wolfenstein 3 is indeed in production at Indiana Jones and the Great Circle devs MachineGames and that Doom makers id Software have started work on their next game after losing a bunch of staff to the mass layoffs across Microsoft's gaming division this year.

"A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations," isn't part of the marketing spiel for either of those games. Instead, it's something Xbox CEO Asha Shama has bellowed amid a rant outlining how she sees the tech giant's future.

In a recent development, the Wolfenstein and id confirmations came as Xbox had a bit of a social media party to commemorate their 25th birthday. Sharma, ever keen to be seen right next to any positive news coming out of the organization, confirmed Wolfenstein 3 is in production by posting a photo showing a few lines from its script. Around the same time, she shouted out Doom: The Dark Ages Revelations' incoming Slaughter Mode, adding that "the team is already working on its next game".

The official id Software account responded to note that this next game is being made by their "teams in Texas and Frankfurt, with game direction once again by Hugo Martin", and that "it'll be some time before [they're] ready to share more".

Industry observers note that we're incredibly excited about our next project, a newly introduced game from our teams in Texas and Frankfurt, with game direction once again by Hugo Martin. It'll be some time before we're ready to share more but we can't wait for you to see what we're working on.

Alongside hollering about these couple of games, Sharma put out a 25th anniversary statement which for the most part does the sort of bigging up of Xbox's past you'd expect. Good times were had, we blazed a trail and made lots of money, etcetera. The final section saw the exec attempt to look forward to the next 25 years for Xbox.

"While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically," she wrote. "As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this.

Industry observers note that "Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today's games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982.".

That certainly sounds a lot like the sales pitch the biggest proponents of generative AI keep wheeling out, while avoiding saying generative AI out loud in the hopes of making it more palatable to folks who might not make the connection. I'm waiting for Sharma to put out another post revealing that she accidentally mixed another section of the Wolfenstein script into her celebratory musings, but I'm not holding my breath.

Xbox parent company Microsoft are still at the moment subject to a BDS movement boycott over their reported ties to the Israeli military.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I thought we'd already gotten our fill of prehistoric creatures on the 2026 movie schedule, thanks to The End of Oak Street. The film sees Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor spending a summer trying to survive a neighborhood full of creatures that should have been extinct for millions of years. Then, as soon as the movie hit streaming, the internet started arguing over footage supposedly showing a pterodactyl flying over Mexico. The timing feels a little too perfect.

The latest monster-of-the-week discussion took off on November 13, when someone posted images to Reddit's r/Cryptozoology forum. The poster claimed the winged creature had been caught on airport security footage in Ciudad Juárez and that additional witnesses had photographs. None of that was verified, but you can probably guess how the comments went.

Recent findings suggest that I'll give the image this much: It's pretty cool. The creature has an enormous wingspan, a long, pointed head, and a silhouette you'd expect to see flying over the Platt family's house in The End of Oak Street. Of course, it also looks suspiciously like something you'd find in Jurassic Park. Several Reddit users noticed that resemblance, too, and weren't particularly convinced.

Recent findings suggest that there's apparently more to the sighting. According to Mexican outlet El Financier, an earlier video, reportedly recorded October 29 in the Anapra area of Ciudad Juárez, reveals a mysterious winged figure flying across the night sky. Jaime Maussan, a Mexican broadcaster known for his interest in UFOs and other unexplained phenomena, picked up the footage and helped spread the story. Before long, additional alleged sightings circulated online, and naturally, the internet had a field day.

No cryptic sighting is worth its weight in dino dung unless the internet loses its collective mind, and the comments weren't disappointing. One commenter with the username r/alfred0t0rnad0 pretty much summed up my feelings:.

I WANT TO BELIEVE, but I just can't.

Somebody else was considerably more enthusiastic about the possibility of prehistoric creatures making a comeback. R/AsadAliShadowhunter wrote:.

At this point, I hope the Dinos are back.

According to recent reports, look, I'm not opposed to a little prehistoric excitement. I'd just prefer anything with a 20-foot wingspan to stay away from my backyard.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Those two comments barely scratch the surface, though. Some users had legitimate questions about the footage, while others were just enjoying the absurdity. Here are a few of my favorites:.

In a recent development, personally, I'm partial to the idea of a prehistoric creature emerging from the hollow Earth for tacos. But the commenters questioning how an entire population of giant flying reptiles could have gone unnoticed for millions of years have a pretty good point.

The End Of Oak Street Ending: Yes, They Had Conversations About The Dog Dying.

According to recent reports, there's also the small matter of what local authorities have said about the footage. EFE's fact-checking team reported Wednesday that Ciudad Juárez's civil protection director, Sergio Rodríguez, dismissed the recordings as digital entertainment content. One widely shared version also appears to show signs of AI manipulation, although the origins of the various clips haven't all been established.

Unfortunately for those of us hoping The End of Oak Street had somehow become a documentary, there's no credible evidence that a pterodactyl is flying around Mexico. Still, I have to admit I've enjoyed watching the internet speculate over the possibility.

The End of Oak Street is now streaming with an HBO Max subscription, which makes it an excellent choice if this whole thing has you craving some cinematic dinosaurs.

Grand Theft Auto VI's Auto Drive Is A Beautiful And Free Version Of Hands-Free Travel

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (333 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI is a game where you spend a lot of time behind the wheel.
  • Industry observers note that this is where Auto Drive comes in.
  • First, you must select a destination.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is a game where you spend a lot of time behind the wheel. Always has been. But sometimes, you just won't feel like actively driving, but you also don't to waste money on a cab.

Industry observers note that this is where Auto Drive comes in. It lets the game take over and drive you where you need to go in real time and all with a cinematic camera that shifts and moves, letting you take in the environment without all that pesky "having to pay attention to the road." Red Dead Redemption 2 had the same feature, and I have fond memories of taking advantage of it to watch Arthur ride his horse through that game's incredible environment. It's a great option in GTAVI, but how to use it and turn it on isn't immediately apparent.

First, you must select a destination. Get the GPS set up to direct you to where you want to go.

Next, start driving. The Auto Drive is smart, but doesn't seem to be smart enough to make three-point turns or back out of parking lots. You need to be on your way before you can turn it on.

Once you're on the path, hold down in the d-pad and press start to activate Cinematic.

According to recent reports, once you've done this you should be able to hold down the Circle button on PlayStation or the B button on Xbox to activate Auto Drive and... voilà! You can sit back and let Jason or Lucia take the wheel. They will drive legally, even stopping at lights, but you can speed them up if they're taking too long.

I am nothing if not entirely predictable. I've waited 13 years to play a latest Grand Theft Auto game and the first thing I do when I finally get around to booting GTA 6—and definitely not spoofing my home address to access it early—is jam a mouse and keyboard into my Xbox Series X just to see.

GTA 5, once it made its way to PC, was always a game I played both with a keyboard and mouse and with a controller plugged in. Keeb and rodent for shooting, especially in the first-person mode, and the controller for just getting about in the game world. It was a real best of both worlds kinda thing that the PC does so well.

It was the same with Red Dead Redemption 2, a game I completely avoided until it finally came to the PC. Keyboard and mouse for runnin' and gunnin' and a controller for horsin' around. Yeehaw.

Industry observers note that so, I was hoping—hoping against hope, really—that I could just do the same with GTA 6. I was hoping that I could just plug in my little Mountain keyboard and my DeathAdder mouse, and it would just work.

It has been revealed that sadly no, there is no mouse and keyboard support for GTA 6. There is for Xbox, and my keyboard works fine just in the home screens, but as soon as you hit the game itself… nada. Keyboard and mouse support is still very much an occasional thing for Microsoft's console. It is supported, but it's on a per-game basis where devs have to actively code support into their Xbox versions of a title in order for a keyboard and mouse to work.

It's not actually that rare—some 450 games, and big games such as Cyberpunk 2077 and Alan Wake 2, have some level of support for one or both peripherals. But it is certainly not something Rockstar has spent any time putting in place when it was spending an extra year optimising the game after the delayed release. Which is a shame, given that the organization has gone to great lengths to add a huge level of detail to its world to the point it almost feels like it's thought of everything.

Recent findings suggest that more frustrating given that right now I bet there are Rockstar developers playing the game on keyboard and mouse in internal PC-only builds of the game. Would I have sacrificed sitting on my comfy sofa playing it writ large on my living room wall through my 4K projector just to sit at my desk with a keyboard and mouse? Maybe. It would have certainly felt like I was playing it on PC.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products.

Industry observers note that something else Rockstar hasn't put into the game is any steering wheel control. Jacob, as a racing fan, tried to get his PlayStation wheelbase running on his PS5 copy of the game… but alas that is unsupported, too. Which was a source of frustration for him as he co-opted his partner in carrying his sim rig into his living room to try it out and now she is refusing to help put it back after his failure.

But this is a situation that might have to change moving forward. The next-gen Xbox machine, codenamed Helix has already been confirmed as being able to play PC games. In a recent interview with Jason Ronald, Xbox VP of Next Gen, this was again reiterated.

"We're very clear on the design goal: Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC," says Ronald. "It is not a PC that can also play console games.".

Sources indicate that this means it's going to have to support PC games, and that potentially means baked in support for keyboard and mouse in the hardware itself, rather than enabled on a per-title basis. After all, PC games kinda take those inputs for granted, no? So, maybe Red Dead Redemption 3 on Project Helix might come with keyboard and mouse support from the get-go, even if it's not necessarily released on PC straight away.

Still, for GTA 6 right now, basically it's controller or nothing, so make sure to get yourself a good pad—that's one of the biggest upgrades I've made to my setup for GTA 6.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It took Battlefield Studios over four months to tell Battlefield 6 players what they can actually expect from the game over the course of this year, in terms of content - but we’re glad to see a plan laid out nonetheless.

The developer unveiled a grand 2026 roadmap, covering three more seasons right now in the works, and a wealth of newly introduced additions across the entire game, including new maps and the introduction of a new theatre of combat.

In a wide-ranging new video dubbed The Year Ahead, members of the Battlefield 6 development team have revealed a lot of new information about the future of the multiplayer shooter, going over plenty of the features and new content coming over the course of this year.

The video confirmed that BF6 has at least three other seasons in the works. Season 3, which begins in May, will be followed by Season 4, and Season 5 later in the year. Season 5 is the most mysterious, which is understandable.

In a recent development, we’ve known about some of what’s coming in Season 3, such as the remake of Golmud Railway (now called Railway to Golmud), but the video also revealed that a remake of Battlefield 3’s Grand Bazaar - now Cairo Bazaar - will also arrive later in the same season. Other exciting additions, such as battle royale solos and ranked play for Redsec are also on the agenda for Season 3.

Recent findings suggest that season 4, set for July, looks to be the biggest so far, with the introduction of naval combat, which will be available across two maps. Tsuru Reef, which is stated to be even larger than Golmud, the largest map in BF6. The Pacific-set map won’t be the only one, as later in the season, another remake will arrive, this time of the iconic Wake Island.

The introduction of naval combat will bring with it a latest dynamic wave system, aircraft carriers with operational flight decks, and new naval vehicles. Custom lobbies and Spectator Mode are also planned for Season 4.

Season 5 will bring three maps to BF6, rather than two, but all of its content remains under wraps.

According to recent reports, perhaps a sour note is that almost all of the maps referenced and shown in the video are remakes of maps from other Battlefield games, or reimagined at the very least. The Battlefield series is no stranger to remaking its own maps, but Battlefield 6 appears to be leaning on it much more than past entries.

If it’s any consolation, however, the map remakes we’ve played so far in Battlefield 6 have gone through major changes that have contributed to giving them a different flow and feel from their classic versions, or even remakes in other BF games.

Over the course of 2026, you can also expect the return of persistent servers, as well as a server browser to find them all - just like the good ol’ days. This includes the ability to host your own, though it’s unclear quite how this is going to work.

Season 3 is set to revealed in the coming days, so you’ll be hearing back from BF Studios in the near future.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • But then I realised that I wasn't looking at a live newsfeed, but merely the Steam page for Horu, a real-time 4X strategy game in which you can "command hundreds of thousands of units across land and space", in the summary of developer David "GlassBeaver" Nadaski.
  • It has been revealed that in development for years, and running on a custom C++ engine, Horu is inspired by 2006 hybrid RTS Star Wars: Empire at War - good, not great, in the words of turncoat jankonaut Graham, and the subject of many mods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that clicking a random link this morning, I was dazzled by the glare of a thousand laser batteries firing simultaneously. My ears trembled beneath the trundle of a million caterpillar tracks. Balls of ice, bolts of lightning, shipments of rare alloys, and cascades of drop pods went screaming down my nerves and detonated in my frontal cortex, painting starlanes across the inside of my skull. "Oh god, they've finally found us!" I yelled, hiding beneath my desk. "I for one welcome our latest galactic overlords!".

But then I realised that I wasn't looking at a live newsfeed, but merely the Steam page for Horu, a real-time 4X strategy game in which you can "command hundreds of thousands of units across land and space", in the summary of developer David "GlassBeaver" Nadaski. There's also a magic system, this being "the spice that makes your enemy's defeat bitter", which is a very genteel way to characterise glaciating a tank formation or conjuring a miniature blackhole.

It has been revealed that in development for years, and running on a custom C++ engine, Horu is inspired by 2006 hybrid RTS Star Wars: Empire at War - good, not great, in the words of turncoat jankonaut Graham, and the subject of many mods. Horu's way of bettering Empire at War is seemingly to add a shedload more of everything. You can engage in a fleet battle that looks like two migrating ant hives colliding, even as a frankly unnecessary quantity of cyborgs pour over the forgeworld beneath and get their shit kicked in by some tornado-summoning sorcerers.

Offensives appear to work like this: any drop ships that push through the fleet battle add meat to the ground invasion, with the option of deploying wormholes to sneak your troops behind the defending armada. On the ground, you're basically out to capture control points. You're allegedly spared from "continuous babysitting" by semi-autonomous squadron commanders and an orders system that lets you queue up objectives, before units engage in battle.

In a recent development, you can still give individual orders to units, but that seems like a recipe for acute wrist injury. There's also a boarding action mechanic whereby your hijackers move through vessels room by room. Again, I struggle to understand how you'll have time and dexterity to oversee such skulduggery when there are a bajillion particle cannons going off all at once.

Outside of combat, there are planets to develop, shipyards to build, spy networks to groom, research trees to water, and stock markets to manipulate. It all looks like business as usual for an imperial 4X. Honestly, I can imagine the maximalist warfaring being a hot mess, and then there's the fact that the dev is running a Kickstarter "to fund the remaining assets needed for a playable build: more spaceships, more units, more animations, more sounds, more music, and everything in between." I've been burned by Kickstarter overpromising before. Still, I can only admire the vindictive intellect that would have me play a little game of FTL inside what looks like one of the larger PvP scraps from Eve Online.

Sources indicate that you can read more on Steam. Release date there is currently none. For an equally populous strategy experience that's closer in style to Supreme Commander, check out Sanctuary: Shattered Space.

Yes, while 19th November 2026 will forever be known as 'GTA 6 Day ', a handful of other games are also braving the launch window and are releasing on Switch today.

We know that your adventures in Leonida will take priority, and that's okay, but we thought it was only right to highlight the other experiences that didn't back down from the big boy's launch plans. We're talking 60fps at 1080p and "enhanced graphics". Sounds ripe for a replay, if you ask us.

Industry observers note that published and developed by room6, this is a roguelike all about gathering cute pixel art plushies to your aid and using their powers to survive a nighttime onslaught of monsters. Need we say more? It seems to strike that balance of cute/creepy pretty well, and we can see it being quite the time sink, with 40 recruitable plushies, 100 items and 20 costumes available to mix up every run.

Those who frequent Japanese merch stalls will no doubt recognise the Sumikkogurashi gang. This one sees the team of adorable little blobs tasked with helping out at onsen inns to ensure their smooth running. There's plenty of minigames and scope to expand the inns further, but come on, the cuteness is the big draw here. Just look at those little guys!

It's The Binding of Isaac again (again). This re-release features all of the game's DLC content and the chance to play it with up to four players online.

Desperate for more throwback shooting after breezing through Boltgun? Auroch Digital has got you covered. After launching on other consoles last month, Warhammer 40,000 Boltgun 2 finally arrives on Switch 2 today with even more strafing, shooting and scary monstrosities. The score features a surprise cameo track from composer Mick Gordon (DOOM, DOOM Eternal, Wolfenstein: The New Order), which is an added bonus for music fans.

According to recent reports, naturally, the eShop will be home to many more debuts today, but the above selection gives a pretty good range of options (and a certain quality that a bunch of the other releases lack). Let us know in the comments if there's another newbie today that we've missed!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By now, you've hopefully had a chance to check out our review of GTA 6 for Xbox Series X elsewhere on Pure Xbox, and it exists because Rockstar gave us multiple weeks' worth of early access to the game ahead of release.
  • According to recent reports, I was the lucky person to take on the review responsibility for the latest Grand Theft Auto, and I've put basically all of my free time into it since late October.
  • Some of these were already known prior to today, whereas others might be brand-fresh information.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By now, you've hopefully had a chance to check out our review of GTA 6 for Xbox Series X elsewhere on Pure Xbox, and it exists because Rockstar gave us multiple weeks' worth of early access to the game ahead of release.

According to recent reports, I was the lucky person to take on the review responsibility for the latest Grand Theft Auto, and I've put basically all of my free time into it since late October. While completing the campaign, I inevitibly came across loads of features that surprised me along the way, so I thought I'd use this opportunity to just highlight a few of them.

Some of these were already known prior to today, whereas others might be brand-fresh information. In any case, here are the specific features (avoiding story spoilers) that surprised me as I was completing GTA 6 on Xbox Series X:.

In a recent development, yeah, there's finally a fuel requirement in a GTA game! It's not too invasive, so don't worry, but if you happen to drive a car around the map for an extensive amount of time, you'll be forced to find a gas station and refuel it (a very short cutscene and a press of the RT button). You can also repair your car at gas stations as well, which certainly comes in handy if you've been smashing it around at high speeds!

You can still break into vehicles the old fashioned way - either stealing it mid-drive or smashing a window to gain access - but you can also use a slim-jim to break the lock, or eventually a key cloner to bypass the security entirely. Be aware of vehicles with trackers though, as if you end up going too slow, the tracker will alert the cops to your location.

According to recent reports, it's not always enough to escape the cops and stay hidden from them for an extended period of time. If you really want to ensure you'll lose their attention, you'll want to either ditch the car or take it to a "Pay 'n' Spray" outlet, as well as change your outfit. It's possible to partially do this by throwing on some sunglasses and a hat, but the clever move is to stash one or more outfits in your car's trunk that you can switch between at a moment's notice.

It has been revealed that while it's impossible to avoid situations in GTA 6 where you'll be engaging in all sorts of criminal activity, you can handle them in various ways. For example, a mission that requires you to take out a bunch of people can be completed by one-shotting them all, but this will raise your criminal profile. Alternatively, leaving your enemies injured but still alive will push you more towards a "Professional" profile. I haven't properly been able to compare how this affects the game yet (I really need to experiment with both sides of the extreme rather than hovering towards the middle), but Rockstar notes it alters how the story, world and Jason / Lucia react to you.

In a recent development, I always love when games get creative with music - South of Midnight was one that really impressed me - and GTA 6 is now one of the best examples I can think of. Basically, you get highly-curated pumping tunes playing in the background during things like shootouts and getaways, while more menacing situations can feature a different vibe of soundtrack, sometimes even with lyrics. You might not quite understand the appeal until you play it, but it's actually one of my favourite latest features. The use of music in certain cutscenes is awesome as well.

I don't know if I can verify this yet for sure, but the radio stations either appear to change their music selection based on where you are on the map, or based on how far you've progressed into the story. As I spent more time in Vice City, I started to notice a much bigger range of songs on the Flash FM channel (my favourite) including everyone from Coldplay to The Ting Tings, whereas those tunes never popped up at the start. Try it for yourself and let me know if I'm right about this!

In a recent development, any GTA game worth its salt has to come with a whole bunch of minigames, and my favourite so far is the addition of minigolf. I believe there are three 18-hole courses dotted around the map in total, and they're beautifully detailed and themed, with genuinely enjoyable holes to play on. There's actual golf as well, but I have to admit I haven't had chance to check it out yet. Pool in the bars is great fun too!

It has been revealed that if you really take your time to play through GTA 6, which I highly recommend you do, you'll truly be able to appreciate just how much effort has gone into some of the seemingly smallest aspects of it. Snapmatic, which is the social media platform on your in-game phone, is constantly being updated with fresh statuses, photos, videos, comments and more, and you could literally just sit just browsing it for ages and enjoying the interactions. There's also a "News" app that regularly gets updated with fresh articles about what's going on in Leonida.

It has been revealed that when you get to a certain mission in GTA 6, you'll be introduced to your first video game inside the game itself, which seems to be a very high-brow parody of modern-day indie hits. There are actually multiple games you can play, including one that's very reminiscent of Xbox title Yet Another Zombie Survivors, and these can either be accessed by turning on your TV or going up to arcade cabinets located in various stores all over the map.

In a recent development, when GTA 5 came out for Xbox 360 back in 2013, one of the big things I can recall is how slow the initial loading screens would be, especially once GTA Online got involved. We obviously haven't got an online component to GTA 6 just yet, but in terms of loading up the single-player game on Xbox Series X, it's actually a very quick process that isn't painful whatsoever. You barely even notice it!

Sources indicate that of course, these aren't the only surprising features you'll run into while playing GTA 6 - there are literally hundreds and hundreds that are waiting to be discovered. I don't want to spoil anything about the story or the details of the missions themselves though, and ultimately this is a game where surprises will continue being revealed long into the future.

Recent findings suggest that for now, just go and enjoy it on your Xbox Series X or Xbox Series S (or PS5), and I urge you to take your time and really let it all soak in. One of the perils of reviewing games is that you have to grind to the finish line, and while that does still give you a great impression of the experience, I already can't wait to go back and spend 100+ hours with it this time.

Recent findings suggest that anything here sound particularly enticing to you? Let us know down in the comments section below.

Recent findings suggest that anyone who's watched an episode of The Bear or a YouTube cooking show immediately recognized a central supporting character in GTA 6, Jason's lovable, rambling redneck friend, Cal. He's obviously Matty Matheson, the chef and actor best-known as Neil Fak on the FX TV show The Bear. And yet, he definitely isn't, because Matheson himself has confirmed he isn't in GTA 6 at all.

Matheson clearly caught wind of the comparisons he's been getting since Cal was revealed in trailers and promotional images a couple of years back, and took to Instagram to dispel the suspicions. "I just wanted to say that I'm not in Grand Theft Auto 6," he says as an image of Cal appears on-screen. "I'm not. That's not me, it's not my voice. But uh, yeah, I don't know... So, it's not me. Have a beautiful day.".

Industry observers note that cal is quickly becoming one of my favorite characters in GTA 6. He's the lovable oaf that every protagonist needs by their side in a rollicking, dangerous adventure like the one Jason and Lucia get into in GTA 6. I say that as a protective preface before the following sentence: I refuse to believe that isn't Matty Matheson. I mean, it definitely isn't his voice or performance, but Cal, in spirit, will always be a digitized Matty Matheson to me, or at least the exaggerated, high-energy persona he assumes in a lot of his videos. Or maybe he's Danny McBride.

Joking aside, it's actually former Saturday Night Live mainstay Bobby Moynihan that plays Cal in GTA 6, according to Vulture, and you know what, that's damn good fit I hadn't even considered before researching for this story.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft 365 isn't quite living up to its name this week, as its services have suffered an extended outage that's knocked the likes of Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for six. As of writing, the organization are finally reporting "encouraging recovery progress in Europe" and are busy "addressing the remaining areas of disruption", but that's only after chunks of November 12th and 13th have seen people, businesses, and institutions left unable to use stuff they rely on.

That latest upgrade was given by Microsoft to the BBC, who've had a live report on the outage running, since it's affected the likes of schools, government services and medical services. IGN and Kotaku's reports differ on whether any Xbox services appear to be affected. The Xbox status support page currently indicates all is swell, but Downdetector does show a recent uptick in reports of complications.

Industry observers note that "We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the matter," Microsoft exec Charles LaManna wrote in response to a support thread on the topic in the early hours of November 13th UK time. "We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.".

As much as it's slightly reassuring that there presently looks to have been no big hack, the time it's taken to deploy proper fixes is concerning, with Microsoft noting some of their early attempts at rectifying things "not taking as expected".

According to recent reports, the debacle has rather emphasised how far from ideal it is that so much key infrastructure across the world runs on one clump of tech which all go down in a heartbeat, but to a certain degree that is the peril of relying on anything. One can only hope that Microsoft's ongoing efforts to fire vast numbers of staff into the sun and embrace AI haven't factored into lots of their services going tits up for an inconvenient amount of time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Diablo 4 is gearing up for its biggest post-launch event yet: the upcoming release of the Lord of Hatred expansion. As was the case with Vessel of Hatred before it, expansion releases alter the seasonal flow in a few ways, and Blizzard has now explained how.

Sources indicate that the game’s next season - its 13th - has been officially revealed as Season of Reckoning. The upcoming season will kick off alongside the expansion’s release next week, and will be available to all players, just like all previous seasons.

Although Season of Reckoning will roll out as normal, the season itself won’t be as meaty, at least when it comes to the sort of gameplay mechanics and themes players have come to expect from each upcoming season.

It has been revealed that you’ll still find the normal Season Rank chase, Smoldering Ashes, and various rewards at each chapter. Season Blessings will also return, but that’s about it for progression outside of the game itself. If it’s any consolation, there are more goals and objectives to tackle this season.

Sources indicate that the even better news is that, according to Blizzard, future seasons will follow the classic format, which makes sense. The newly introduced season will come with a battle pass, of course, featuring four Reliquaries, as usual. The first Reliquary is free, while the others are paid.

Blizzard has also confirmed the the pre-load for Lord of Hatred is available now on all platforms. Even if you’re not getting the expansion, patch 3.0.0's pre-load includes all expansion content regardless, so you may as well pre-download it to be ready for April 27/28. On launch day, you’ll also need to download a smaller patch, version 3.0.1.

According to recent reports, in case you missed it, we published our Lord of Hatred review earlier in the week. Give it a read if you’re curious about the expansion’s impact on the narrative, and how it changes core Diablo 4 gameplay.

Recent findings suggest that among the book-to-screen adaptations I'm most excited for in 2027 is The Nightingale. Based on Kristin Hannah's brilliant novel, the story follows two sisters in France whose lives go in different directions during World War II, and the choices they have to make along the way.

Recent findings suggest that directed by Michael Morris and starring real-life sisters Dakota and Elle Fanning, The Nightingale follows their characters' stories as they find themselves getting more involved in what's going around them as the Nazis invade France. While Hannah's novel is historical fiction, the book is inspired by true accounts of the war.

In a recent development, the more I've learned about World War II, particularly in looking at the impact it had on different regions of the world, the more interested I've become in hearing stories about the involvement of women in the war. Naturally, I was drawn to Hannah's novel. (She also wrote an amazing historical fiction novel called The Women, which is set during the Vietnam War that I highly recommend.) Exciting, emotional and powerful, The Nightingale absolutely lived up to the hype (4.6+ out of 5 on Goodreads with over 2 million ratings?!), and I can't wait to see the movie.

In The Nightingale, Vianne (Dakota Fanning) is trying to keep her daughter safe as the Nazis begin to occupy France. Meanwhile, her younger sister, Isabelle (Elle Fanning), wants to take a more active role in what's going on, and finds herself joining the resistance. While both sisters take a very different approach to survival during this turbulent and dangerous time, the story really shows the way courage can emerge in different ways.

It has been revealed that with just a minute's worth of footage, this latest teaser gives us a good look at what these two sisters face as their entire world is upended by this war. Vianne is determined to keep her family safe, while Isabelle -- despite her very young age -- can't stand by and not try to help make a difference. In the end, both women end up finding themselves faced with dangerous situations and impossible choices that require quick thinking and more courage than most could muster when push comes to shove. Whether they're protecting children and innocents or going undercover to help with the resistance, the story of these sisters indicates the impact one woman can make amidst the chaos of war.

Of course, the teaser leaves off with "She'll need a codename," which points directly to the title of the movie.

I'm excited about everything to do with this adaptation, from the source material, to the stars, to what we're seeing here. While many World War II movies emphasize the invasions and battles, stories like The Nightingale -- whether fiction, non-fiction, or inspired by true events -- remind us of the impact of war on the spaces in between the battles, and the civilians who find (sometimes crucial) ways to help.

Corsair Sabre V3 Pro PureVector Ergo review

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pcgamer

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the aim-assisting PureVector technology in this mouse promises a lot, but in my case it fails to deliver, as my aim doesn't improve from turning it on.
  • According to recent reports, PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you.
  • Corsair is continuing the 2026 trend of brands pushing out newly introduced and innovative mouse technologies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the aim-assisting PureVector technology in this mouse promises a lot, but in my case it fails to deliver, as my aim doesn't improve from turning it on. It's a solid, lightweight, competitive mouse regardless, but it's too expensive for what it is without delivering the PureVector promise.

According to recent reports, PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Corsair is continuing the 2026 trend of brands pushing out newly introduced and innovative mouse technologies. In this case, it's all in the 'PureVector' part of the name. In partnership with AimLabs, Corsair has made a mouse that can adjust sensitivity in different directions to tailor it to your movements and help you aim better.

That's the claim, anyway. In practice, I've found that PureVector hasn't improved my aim, both subjectively while gaming and objectively based on multiple AimLabs tests. Some pro players that Corsair highlights claim it's helped them, so your mileage may vary.

It has been revealed that apart from PureVector, though, the mouse itself deserves some attention, as it's still a very performant, lightweight mouse for competitive gaming. It has some upgrades compared to its predecessor, the Sabre V2 Pro, too.

Recent findings suggest that ✅ You want to try the latest tech: You might get better results than I did with PureVector. It tailors sensor sensitivity in different directions based on how you aim.

❌ You want good value for the basics: If you just want a comfy mouse with solid build quality that performs well, you can find something of better value elsewhere.

The aim-assisting PureVector technology in this mouse promises a lot, but in my case it fails to deliver, as my aim doesn't improve from turning it on. It's a solid, lightweight, competitive mouse regardless, but it's too expensive for what it is without delivering on the PureVector promise.

Replacement skates, USB-A to USB-C cable, wireless dongle, AimLabs PureVector software integration.

It has been revealed that in most ways, the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector Ergo is your standard competitive gaming mouse: lightweight, few frills, simple design, good sensor. It is lighter than most competitive mice with a solid shell, though a little heavier than its predecessor, the Sabre V2 Pro.

Setting aside the PureVector aiming shenanigans for a moment, probably the biggest improvement compared to the Sabre V2 Pro is its battery life, which has been doubled. Apart from that, you're getting a 42,000 DPI sensor, optical clicks, and some bigger replacement skates included in the box.

According to recent reports, now we come to the main attraction: PureVector. Corsair has designed the mouse's internals and firmware to permit different sensitivities in different directions. So, for instance, it can move slightly slower horizontally than vertically.

Corsair has worked with AimLabs to let you test your aiming in the latter software and then have the mouse adjust your directional sensitivity for you. The PureVector software within AimLabs has been made with the help of a bunch of aiming data (over 4 billion data points, apparently) and machine learning. The end result is, in theory, a mouse that can tailor its sensitivity in different directions to stop you over-shooting or under-shooting your target.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products.

Again, in theory, this should also save you time when you aim, and Corsair claims it can save more time than reducing the latency of clicks—the latter is, for example, what we see the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike and X3 Superstrike focusing on.

Recent findings suggest that it's worth noting that Corsair highlights a number of pro players who say they've benefitted from this new tech. However, for my part, I haven't noticed a difference.

Recent findings suggest that for reference, I play Counter-Strike 2 at about FaceIt Level 7 or Premier 18–20,000 rating (approx. top 15%). I'm far from a pro, but I'm far from the worst. In-game, I didn't notice any difference between my aim with PureVector set up and with it disabled.

I also repeatedly tested my aim in the AimLabs SpiderShot Precision test, and I actually had slightly better results using another mouse without PureVector (the SteelSeries Sensei Pro), and the latter mouse my hand was less familiar with.

Industry observers note that more than this, though, I can't help but feel that it's a bit of a band-aid solution to poor aim. If you're overshooting your shots when you aim left, for instance, you could get PureVector to lower your sensitivity in that direction. But why not instead work on training your hand not to overshoot? That way, having good aim won't be dependent on using this one mouse, and you can get used to aiming consistently in different directions.

PureVector aside, the Sabre V3 Pro performs well. The sensor is great and feels very responsive. Ditto the new optical mouse clicks. I have no complaints about its performance as a general mouse, I just don't see the use in PureVector myself. Of course, your mileage may vary, as it seems to have for some pro players.

One area where the Sabre V3 Pro does particularly shine, just like the Sabre V2 Pro, is in its light weight. This latest iteration feels even sturdier than the previous one and still manages to be lighter than most competitive gaming mice.

Battery life is a definite selling point of the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector. It's a lot better than I was expecting. The Sabre V2 Pro can only manage about 70 hours at 1 kHz, and this new one doubles that to 140 hours.

I think Corsair has struck a great balance here, because it's not as light as the V2—which was 36 g—but 41 g is still incredibly light, and I'd much rather have the bigger battery than shave off those few extra grams. You're not getting any fancy wireless charging or hot-swappable batteries here, but 140 hours of battery life is great.

The Corsair Sabre V3 Pro PureVector Ergo is, as its excruciatingly long name suggests, pretty ergonomic. It's not the biggest ergo mouse I've used—the Zowie EC2-DW and SteelSeries Rival Pro both feel a bit bigger in-hand—but it still feels comfy under my medium-sized palm.

There's also a non-ergo, symmetrical version for the same price, and you can get carbon fiber or magnesium versions for each, if you're willing to spend even more ($200 and $230, respectively).

In a recent development, I like the lightweight ergonomic version, though. Its slightly smaller size, combined with its light weight, also means holding it in a fingertip or claw grip doesn't feel too bad, which isn't something you can say about many ergonomic mice. Palm grip is still the main intention here, though. Playing Counter-Strike on low sensitivity feels great.

According to recent reports, build quality is decent, too, which is a bit of a relief because the previous version, the Sabre V2 Pro, sacrificed some on this front to achieve its 'ultralight' status. There's no creak or flex along the sides, and only a slight bit of flex on the underside. The side buttons feel great, with no pre-travel, and the scroll wheel has well-defined steps.

Sources indicate that there is some pre-travel to the left- and right-mouse buttons, however, and they don't feel as satisfying to press as some other mice like the Razer Viper V4 Pro or SteelSeries Rival Pro. They're far from bad, just not quite up to the standard of some other expensive gaming mice I've tried.

The version I've got here, the 'Ergo' one, is pretty plain and looks quite similar to its predecessor, the Sabre V2 Pro. It's plain white, with only some very subtle grey accents. I'm fine with that, as the focus is on performance and comfort.

Any extra aesthetic fancies are likely to add to the weight, which isn't worth the sacrifice for this kind of mouse. As with most ultralight mice, you know what you're getting aesthetically, and it's minimal.

In a recent development, this mouse uses the same software as the previous V2 Pro. What's noteworthy is the software is browser-based—there's no locally-installable app to use. That's mainly because you're expected to just set it and go, without returning to adjust things.

You can set up profiles to toggle between DPI using a mouse button combination, however. And the web software can be used offline if you install it as an app in your browser, so internet outages shouldn't cause any problems.

Sources indicate that the web hub is basic but gets the job done. The battery indicator isn't very precise, only showing a tiny icon and no percentage numbers, but that's my only complaint.

The AimLabs integration is perfectly fine, too. Assuming you've got it installed on Steam, you can allow the web hub to boot it up for you from there, or boot it up yourself. Once in, you can navigate to PureVector and let it run you through the aim training to adjust your sensitivity in different sweep directions. It's intuitive, and the directional charts it highlights are clear enough.

Sources indicate that at $180/£160, the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector Ergo is an expensive mouse. It joins the likes of the G Pro X2/X3 Superstrike, Viper V4 Pro, DeathAdder V4 Pro, SteelSeries Rival Pro, and other high-end, competitive gaming mice.

Can it compete with these? In my opinion, not quite. These other gaming mice each have extra features and new technologies that go some way towards justifying the very high price tags. The Superstrikes have analogue clicks, the Viper V4 Pro has FrameSync, the Rival Pro has hot-swappable batteries and UWB connectivity.

Recent findings suggest that the DeathAdder V4 Pro doesn't have anything too fancy like that, but is a very solid gaming mouse. I'd class the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector in this category, alongside the DeathAdder. That's because while the PureVector technology is indeed very latest, I haven't found it to have much of an impact, and so I'm left considering its merits as a general competitive gaming mouse, setting aside this new aim assist tech.

There are merits to it that justify a price tag above $100: light weight, comfy ergonomic shape, optical clicks, responsive scroll wheel, great battery life. But not enough to justify $180—not without something extra, which PureVector promises but, in my case, fails to deliver. Unless, that is, you're set on getting a mouse as light as this one is that still has a sturdy shell.

Recent findings suggest that you could instead, for instance, go for something like the Mchose K7 V2 Ultra+ for about $90. Or a Pulsar mouse like the Pulsar X2 CrazyLight for $130, which sometimes drops to about $100 on sale.

According to recent reports, if you fancy spending the extra to try it out for yourself and see if you can get the kinds of benefits the pros that Corsair highlights espouse, go for it. But for my money, I'd be opting for a cheaper lightweight mouse, or one with better build quality like the Viper V4 Pro.
